evidence.label: sec:p15-w02c-p15-029-romeijn (thesis, plan, purpose, claim types, scope)
Carnapian logic as non-ampliative inference; why hypotheses are absent

components.gap: The source's own definition of the two disciplines and of their relation, p. 625, is not reconstructed. Romeijn defines statistics as a mathematical discipline describing procedures for deriving results about a population from sample data, whose results include decisions to reject or accept a hypothesis about the population, the determination of probability assignments over such hypotheses and predictions on future samples; he defines an inductive logic as a system of inference relating propositions on data to propositions extending beyond them (predictions over future data, general conclusions on data); and he states that both are calculi for getting from the given data to propositions or results that transcend the data. Lines 595-604 state only the chapter's question and thesis, and lines 659-662 give only the p. 626 inductive-inference example; the inferential tasks of statistics and the stated parallel are absent.

sec:p15-w02c-p15-029-rj-assessment (conclusion, chronology of cited works, interpretations, limitations)

components.gap: The historical argument of p. 625 for why inductive logic and statistics evolved more or less separately is narrowed. Romeijn gives two reasons: (i) partly, objections to viewing statistics, especially classical statistical procedures, as inferential; (ii) more importantly, the domination of inductive logic by the Carnapian programme and statisticians' failure to recognise Carnapian inductive logic as a discipline much like their own, with the mutual misunderstanding traced to the different roles of hypotheses in the two programmes. Lines 599-602 say only that the disciplines 'grew apart chiefly because statistical hypotheses ... have no place in Carnap's inductive logic', omitting reason (i) and the Carnapian-dominance and non-recognition claims of reason (ii). Secondary: the general idea Romeijn gives for the fiducial region (p. 646: define a set R of parameter values within which the data are not too unlikely, and say that the true parameter value most likely lies within it) is not stated at lines 1576-1583, which go directly to the role swap in (20).

components.gap: One comparison of p. 640 is omitted. After the Jeffreys example Romeijn says that the results of a Neyman-Pearson procedure depend on the whole probability assignment over the sample space and that, from the perspective of an inductive logician, the procedure may therefore seem 'a remarkable procedure' (citing Jeffreys a second time); his following 'But it must be emphasised that Neyman-Pearson statistics was never intended as an inference in disguise' answers that evaluation. Lines 1193-1217 and 1255-1260 give the example, the first Jeffreys complaint and the reply, but not the inductive logician's evaluation that the reply answers. All other worked cases, limitations, comparisons and claim-type distinctions of the chapter are present.
